extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent prosecutors and attorneys handling life-sciences patents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the Mayo/Alice subject-matter-eligibility framework (Steps 2A and 2B per USPTO guidance) to life‑sciences method claims, with emphasis on how to determine if a claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception and whether it recites an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Mayo/Alice two-step framework (USPTO Steps 2A and 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: These cases do not change the subject matter eligibility framework; apply the two‑step Mayo/Alice framework (Steps 2A and 2B as set out in the USPTO's subject matter eligibility guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the USPTO's subject matter eligibility guidance (2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance, July 2015 Update, May 2016 memoranda and training examples). The memo states the USPTO's guidance and training examples are consistent with the Federal Circuit rulings discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A 'directed to' analysis must examine the claim's focus/essence
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'directed to' analysis of a process claim requires more than 'merely identify[ing] a patent‑ineligible concept underlying the claim' and instead requires an analysis of whether 'the end result of the process, the essence of the whole, was a patent‑ineligible concept.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying Step 2A, assess the claim as a whole to determine its focus (the end result/essence). Do not stop at identifying an underlying natural phenomenon; determine whether the claimed end result itself is an observation/detection (ineligible) or a process producing a practical outcome (may be eligible). Example: the cryopreservation claims were focused on a process producing multi‑cryopreserved viable hepatocytes and thus were not directed to a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish claims that apply a natural law from claims that merely observe/identify it
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'amounted to nothing more than observing or identifying the ineligible concept itself' are distinguishable from claims that apply a law of nature to achieve a practical result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim 'employed their natural discovery to create a new and improved way' of achieving a result (e.g., preserving cells), that application can weigh toward eligibility. Conversely, claims that are effectively limited to detecting or correlating a natural phenomenon (without more) are likely directed to a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims reciting methods of producing things or treating disease are often not 'directed to' a judicial exception when focused on achieving a desired outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims focused on a process for achieving a desired outcome (for example, methods of producing preparations or treating disease) are generally not directed to a judicial exception merely because they involve a natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim's recited process steps meaningfully apply the natural law to produce a practical result (e.g., fractionating, recovering, and cryopreserving to make a preparation of multi‑cryopreserved viable hepatocytes). If so, Step 2A may support eligibility, as with 'thousands of other claims that recite methods of producing things or methods of treating disease.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — inventive concept requires more than routine or conventional steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim is directed to a natural phenomenon under Step 2A, it must recite an 'inventive concept' under Step 2B; routine, well‑understood, conventional activity previously engaged in by researchers does not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factual findings about whether the additional claim steps (e.g., amplifying and detecting) are routine and conventional. Example: in Sequenom the amplifying and detecting steps were held routine/conventional and thus insufficient to transform the natural phenomenon into patent‑eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Federal Circuit panel decisions appropriately and note limitations of precedential weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel decisions (e.g., Rapid Litigation Management, Sequenom) inform analysis but have limits; for example, the denial of certiorari in Sequenom leaves the Federal Circuit panel decision in place but 'does not elevate its significance' beyond that status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the procedural posture and precedential weight of relevant decisions when applying the eligibility framework; rely primarily on the USPTO guidance and established framework while noting helpful points from decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow USPTO subject matter eligibility guidance and consult subject matter experts as needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Life sciences method claims should continue to be treated in accordance with the USPTO's subject matter eligibility guidance (most recently updated in May 2016).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer questions to Technology Center subject matter experts or your SPE when guidance or case law application is unclear.
